root.note: The chain Sanskrit → Persian shakar → Arabic sukkar → Medieval Latin → Italian is the standard account.

history: Sugar travelled a long road before it reached the Italian kitchen. The oldest form we can name is Sanskrit śarkarā, which meant ‘grit’ or ‘gravel’ and then the gritty crystals of cane sugar. Persian turned it into shakar, and Arabic into sukkar. Arab growers planted sugar cane around the Mediterranean, in Sicily among other places, and Italian traders carried the product and the word north. Medieval Latin wrote zuccarum, and Italian says zucchero. The sound ‘zz’ in the middle is typical of words that came in through Arabic. You will hear it at the bar, in ‘un caffè con o senza zucchero?’, and on the label zuccheri in the nutrition table.
historyEinfach: Zucchero comes from Arabic sukkar, which came from Persian and Sanskrit. The old word meant ‘grit’, because sugar looks like small hard grains. Arab farmers grew sugar cane near the Mediterranean, and the word came to Italian with the trade. English sugar, French sucre and Spanish azúcar are relatives.

elsewhere.text: English took the word from Old French in the Middle Ages. German Zucker comes from Italian, and Spanish azúcar keeps the Arabic article al- at the front.
